expected_points: Self-reported daily sedentary screen time did not change significantly before versus during the pandemic (about 6.2 vs 6.7 h/day, p = 0.14)
This contrasts with studies reporting more sedentary time in the general population during the pandemic; the authors suggest unrestricted outdoor riding in the Canadian spring helped
expected_limitations: Small online sample (n = 32) from Canada
Self-reported screen time only, with recall of pre-pandemic behaviour

evidence.quote: No significant differences were observed for time engaged in sedentary behavior before versus during the pandemic (6.15 + 2.6 v. 6.73 + 2.5 h; p ¼ 0.14).
The results of the current research suggest that the current pandemic did not impact the amount of time of our unique sample engaging in sedentary screen time.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: Only mcl-006 measured sitting (screen) time in masters cyclists before and during the pandemic.

question: Do female masters cyclists eat differently from male masters cyclists?
population_applicability: masters_cyclists: direct match, Canadian Masters cyclists, mean age 47 (12 men, 20 women)
expected_points: Women consumed less energy, protein, carbohydrate, fat, fibre, sugar, saturated fat, cholesterol, potassium, sodium and omega-3 than men, but more vitamin K and caffeine
The pandemic-era drops in fibre, vitamin A, folate, potassium and omega-3 were driven by the women, the rise in vitamin C by the men; the rise in alcohol was not sex-specific
expected_limitations: Small sample (12 men, 20 women)
Food frequency questionnaire with recall; absolute intakes not adjusted for body size or energy expenditure

evidence.quote: A difference between males and females was observed for energy (p < 0.001), protein (p < 0.001), carbohydrate (p ¼ 0.002), fiber (p ¼ 0.02), sugar (p ¼ 0.003), fat (p < 0.001), saturated fat (p < 0.001), cholesterol (p ¼ 0.02), vitamin K (p ¼ 0.003), potassium (p ¼ 0.02), sodium (p ¼ 0.03), omega-3 (p < 0.011) and caffeine (p ¼ 0.007), with females consuming lower amounts of all, except for vitamin K and caffeine.

Decreases in fiber (p ¼ 0.01), vitamin A (p ¼ 0.01), folate (p ¼ 0.01), potassium (p ¼ 0.003) and omega-3 (p ¼ 0.04) were driven by females, while increased intakes of vitamin C were driven by males (p ¼ 0.04) during the pandemic.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-006 reports measured dietary intake by sex in masters cyclists; mcl-009 discusses sex and protein requirements, not what athletes eat.

question: Do cyclists become less efficient on the bike as they get older?
population_applicability: masters_endurance_athletes: narrative review; key comparison is master (60 y) vs young (28 y) triathletes
expected_points: VO2max is the determinant most affected by age; economy and lactate threshold decline less
Findings on cycling efficiency with age are inconsistent (both increases and reductions reported)
One study found cycling efficiency 11% lower in 60-year-old than in 28-year-old triathletes
expected_limitations: Mini review, not a systematic analysis
Few studies, differing in age and fitness of the athletes; triathletes rather than pure cyclists

evidence.quote: Exercise economy and the exercise intensity at which a high fraction of VO2max can be sustained (i.e., lactate threshold), seem to decline to a lesser extent with advancing age.
For example, with cycling efficiency, an increase or a possible reduction (Sacchetti et al., 2010; Louis et al., 2012; Brisswalter et al., 2014) in efficiency with advanced age has been observed.

Interestingly, a recent study testing young (28 years) and master (60 years) triathletes showed that cycling efficiency was lower (−11%) and energy cost of running was greater (+11%) in the master compared with young triathletes (Peiffer et al., 2016); but when scaled to lean body mass, changes were more pronounced during the run (+22%).

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-007 directly reviews cycling efficiency with age; mcl-012 (women, mostly running economy) and mcl-008 (running economy) are related; mcl-003 measured efficiency in veteran cyclists but not in relation to age.

question: Does the performance gap between men and women get bigger or smaller in older age groups of endurance athletes?
population_applicability: masters_endurance_athletes: runners and triathletes; no cycling-specific data in the papers graded 2
expected_points: mcl-007: several studies in running and triathlon show the sex difference widens with age, partly amplified by lower participation and depth among older women; at the New York marathon, age-group differences have not differed since 2000
mcl-008: a recent comparison of American road running events found the sex gap narrows with increasing age
The evidence is mixed, so a correct answer should not claim a single clear direction
expected_limitations: Based on race results and cited studies, not new data in either review
Mostly running and triathlon; participation and depth of fields confound physiology

evidence.quote: Several studies have shown that the gender difference in endurance performance increases with advanced age.

For example, at the New-York marathon, differences between men and women in running times decreased for older age groups during the last three decades but since 2000 the differences have not significantly differed across age groups (Lepers and Cattagni, 2012).
In a comparison of American road running events, it was recently shown that the sex gap in performance decreases with increased age [44].

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-007 reports a widening or stabilising gap and mcl-008 a narrowing one, so both are needed for the full picture; mcl-002 (track cyclists), mcl-013 (muscle function) and mcl-012 (determinants) show similar declines by sex but do not address the performance gap directly. mcl-008 graded 1 at review: its sentence cites another study rather than reporting its own result.

question: If a masters cyclist has to stop training for a few weeks or months, how fast is aerobic fitness lost and how quickly does it come back?
population_applicability: different population: detraining data mostly from young endurance-trained athletes and healthy non-athletes; retraining data from older men and one female masters athlete; no cyclists
expected_points: VO2max falls almost linearly from a few days after stopping, by as much as about 20% after 12 weeks
Resuming training can restore a VO2max loss equal to at least a decade of ageing within a few weeks
Training breaks cause a much faster drop than the gradual age-related decline
expected_limitations: Narrative review; the authors note the (re)uptake findings come mainly from non-masters athletes
Few studies, small groups, mostly men

evidence.quote: An almost linear VO2max decrease was observed in studies on young and older athletes, as well as non-athletes, starting a few days after training cessation, with a decline of as much as −20% after 12 weeks.
In summary, a VO2max loss corresponding to aging-related decline of at least one aging decade can be restored by appropriate training (re)uptake within a couple of weeks.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-008 is the only paper on training cessation and resumption, but its data are mostly from non-masters populations; mcl-006 found no fitness change because training did not stop.

question: Do masters athletes eat as much protein after training as younger athletes do?
population_applicability: masters_athletes: older triathletes and mixed-discipline masters athletes; not cycling-specific
expected_points: Masters athletes self-report lower post-exercise meal protein intakes than younger athletes and may eat suboptimal daily amounts (below about 1.31 g/kg/day)
After endurance exercise, younger athletes ate close to the newer ~0.5 g/kg target while older athletes were below it (~0.4 vs 0.3 g/kg)
Half of older triathletes did not know the optimal post-exercise protein dose
expected_limitations: Self-reported intakes, prone to under-reporting
Narrative review drawing on few, small studies

evidence.quote: However, Master athletes self-report lower post- exercise meal protein intakes than their younger counterparts [179] and may generally consume suboptimal daily intakes (i.e. < 1.31 g/kg/day) [103], although one must be mindful of the general propensity for under-reporting in a range of dietary assessment strategies [180].

These lower intakes may also reflect a lack of knowledge on the part of some athletes as 50% of older triathletes responded “I don’t know” when asked about an optimal post-exercise protein dose, whereas only 22% responded with (at the time of its publication) the recommended 20–25 g protein [179].

Importantly, in light of a recent post-endurance exercise protein dose–response study [114], younger athletes on average consumed close to the recommended intake of ~ 0.5 g/kg, whereas older adults were below this new target (i.e. ~ 0.4 vs. 0.3 g/kg, respectively) [179].

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-009 compares masters and younger athletes' protein intakes; mcl-006 reports masters cyclists' absolute protein intake without a younger comparison; mcl-008 gives recommendations, not intakes.

question: Does eating more protein help masters athletes recover from hard workouts that cause muscle damage?
population_applicability: masters_athletes: masters endurance athletes after downhill running; not cycling-specific
expected_points: It has been suggested masters athletes may need more protein after muscle-damaging exercise because their muscle function recovers more slowly than in younger athletes
In one study, masters athletes given 3 x 0.6 g/kg protein after 30 min of downhill running lost slightly less strength (~3.6% vs ~8.6%) than with 3 x 0.3 g/kg
Such high intakes may be hard to sustain, and maximising muscle protein synthesis does not always improve recovery of muscle function
expected_limitations: Few small studies, using downhill running in masters athletes
Narrative review; short-term outcomes only

evidence.quote: From a practical standpoint, it has been suggested that protein requirements may be greater in Master athletes after strenuous bouts of exercise that may elicit some degree of acute muscle damage given the reported delay in the restora- tion of muscle function relative to younger athletes [122].
had a slightly attenuated decrease in muscle strength (~ 3.6 vs ~ 8.6%, respectively) compared to the lower protein condition [124].

However, it should be noted that optimizing rates of MyoPS does not always align with enhanced recovery of muscle function [125, 126], highlight- ing the need for additional research that may promote the restoration of exercise performance and/or optimize training adaptations outside of what is currently recommended for muscle protein remodeling [127].

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-009 reviews protein and recovery after damaging exercise in masters athletes; mcl-010 cites blunted muscle protein synthesis after downhill running in master triathletes and mcl-008 links protein intake to muscle-damage markers in masters runners; mcl-011 studies recovery but not protein.

question: Are men in their 60s and 70s who have done endurance training for decades stronger or leaner than untrained men of the same age?
population_applicability: masters_athletes: endurance-trained men aged 60-80 (3 cyclists, 4 runners) vs untrained men
expected_points: In mcl-010, lean mass, fat mass, body fat and other baseline characteristics did not differ between masters athletes and untrained controls; only training background differed
Knee-extension one-repetition maximum strength did not differ significantly between the groups
Reviews describe masters athletes as having strength and body composition on par with young untrained adults, so the small study is not the whole picture
expected_limitations: Very small sample (7 vs 8 men); the authors' earlier, larger cohort found lower fat mass and greater muscle index in masters athletes
Body composition by bioelectrical impedance; men only

evidence.quote: No significant differences were apparent in any of the baseline characteristics between the groups, with the exception of exercise training background.

No significant difference was apparent between OC and MA in bilateral knee extension 1RM strength and total exercise volume completed (the product of sets × repetition × load) was similar between OC and MA.

For example, a com- prehensive review and meta-analysis by McKendry et al. [8] demonstrated that Master athletes’ aerobic capacity, muscle strength, and body composition are generally on par with young, untrained adults.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-010 directly compares strength and body composition of endurance-trained masters and untrained age-matched men; the others give related evidence on muscle size, strength or power in masters athletes without this exact comparison.

question: How much does a single hard leg-strength session raise muscle protein building over the following two days in men over 60?
population_applicability: masters_athletes: men aged 60-80, endurance-trained (cyclists and runners) and untrained
expected_points: One unaccustomed bout of leg extensions raised myofibrillar protein synthesis over 48 h by about 10% above rest (about 1.46-1.47 to 1.60-1.61 %/day)
The increase was the same in endurance-trained masters athletes and untrained older men
expected_limitations: Small sample (15 men)
Single session of one exercise, with 20 g whey after exercise and a controlled diet; muscle protein breakdown not measured

evidence.quote: RE significantly increased iMyoPS above rest in both OC (1.60 ± 0.08%·day−1, P < 0.01) and MA (1.61 ± 0.08%·day−1, P < 0.01), with no difference between groups.

whilst rested-state iMyoPS rates were similar between MA and OC and comparable to values reported elsewhere in older individuals (∼1.4–1.5%·day−1) (McGlory et al., 2018; Bell et al., 2019), the capacity to increase iMyoPS rates in response to unaccustomed RE did not differ between MA and OC (∼10% increase over 48 h post-exercise).

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-010 measured 48-h muscle protein synthesis after one strength session in older men; mcl-009 reports acute post-exercise responses in older untrained men only as background.

question: Have masters cyclists been getting faster over the decades compared with younger riders?
population_applicability: different population: masters marathon runners and Ironman triathletes; no cycling-only performance trends
expected_points: Over recent decades, performances of master athletes (over 40) in endurance and ultra-endurance events improved faster than those of younger athletes
Gains were largest in the oldest groups (over 60), e.g. Ironman men aged 60-64 improved by 20% from 1986 to 2010
expected_limitations: Data come from marathon and triathlon results, not cycling races
Descriptive race-result trends in a mini review; the reasons offered (participation, training, coaching, nutrition, equipment) are speculative

evidence.quote: The increased participation of master athletes (i.e., >40 years old) in endurance and ultra-endurance events (>6 h duration) over the past few decades has been accompanied by an improvement in their performances at a much faster rate than their younger counterparts.
The improvement in performance of master athletes is more pronounced for the oldest age group categories (>60 years).
For example, at the Hawaii Ironman triathlon, the male 60–64 year age group triathletes improved their performance by 20% during 1986–2010 the period.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-007 documents faster improvement in master runners and triathletes; mcl-009 only notes that master triathlete performance may not have peaked. No paper has cycling-only trends.

question: When doing repeated 30-second all-out sprints, how much does the length of the easy-spinning break affect power for riders in their late 40s compared with younger riders?
population_applicability: masters_cyclists: partial match, older group mean age 47 (well-trained cyclists and triathletes; authors limit conclusions to about age 50)
expected_points: In both age groups, power fell most across the four sprints with 1-minute recoveries and least with 10-minute recoveries
Older and younger athletes did not differ in peak power, average power or fatigue with any recovery length
The authors concluded that longer active recoveries (3 to 10 minutes or more) help both age groups keep power high in every sprint
expected_limitations: Small study (12 older and 12 younger athletes) with men and women analysed together
Older group averaged 47 years; the authors say the findings apply up to about age 50
Only four 30-second all-out sprints with active (not passive) recovery were tested

evidence.quote: For both age groups, the overall performance decline was most significant in the one-minute HIIT protocol.

These findings also show that an active recovery of well over 3 to 10 min is recommendable for both younger and older athletes in order to achieve high power output in each interval and to minimize fatigue-induced power loss.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: Only mcl-011 compares recovery lengths between repeated all-out sprints in older and younger riders. mcl-005 (continuous exercise, heart rate variability) and mcl-015 (fixed 2-minute recoveries) do not test break length.

question: Do well-trained riders in their 40s and 50s put out less sprint power than riders in their 20s with the same aerobic fitness?
population_applicability: masters_cyclists: partial match, older group mean age 47 vs younger group mean 24.5, matched for aerobic fitness
expected_points: Older athletes had lower peak power per kg of body mass at baseline, but they also carried more body fat; peak power per kg of fat-free mass did not differ
Across the repeated 30-second sprint sessions there were no significant age differences in peak power, average power or fatigue
expected_limitations: Groups were deliberately matched for aerobic fitness and training volume, so the study does not show typical age-related decline
Small sample (12 per group) with mixed sexes; older group mean age 47

evidence.quote: Considering peak power output relative to FFM, there were no sig- nificant differences between the age groups
No significant differences were found between the groups in PP, AP, and fatigue (%) throughout the different HIIT protocols (Table 2).

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-011 directly compares sprint power in fitness-matched older and younger riders. mcl-002 shows jump power and sprint performance falling with age across master track cyclists but has no young comparison group; mcl-005 and mcl-001 do not compare sprint power by age.

question: Does going through menopause change aerobic fitness in women who keep competing in endurance sports?
population_applicability: masters_cyclists: women masters endurance athletes aged 40-65 (runners, cyclists, swimmers and triathletes)
expected_points: The effect of menopause on aerobic capacity in women masters athletes is unclear because it has rarely been studied
Few studies measured estrogen, none measured progesterone, and menopause hormone therapy was seldom controlled, which may have masked effects
Training volume, not menopause, emerged as the clearer predictor of aerobic capacity
expected_limitations: Scoping review of 29 mostly cross-sectional studies, many with small samples
Menopause status was often poorly defined

evidence.quote: Training volume emerged as a predictor of aerobic capacity, but the effects of menopause were unclear.
Despite this, few studies quantified estrogen and none considered progesterone levels or the complex interactions between multiple hormones [2].
These gaps leave women masters athletes without clear evidence to guide decisions on hormonal health or menopause management.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-012 is the only paper that examines menopause and endurance determinants in women masters athletes. mcl-009 discusses menopause only for muscle mass and protein needs; mcl-008 and mcl-007 do not mention menopause.

question: Do lactate test results change as women endurance athletes get older, and what does that mean for setting training zones?
population_applicability: masters_cyclists: women masters endurance athletes aged 40-65 (mostly runners)
expected_points: Evidence is limited and mixed: most studies found peak lactate stayed stable with age, though one found a decrease
Lactate threshold as a percentage of VO2max tended to rise with age, a shift that seems to occur independently of training adaptation in masters athletes
The authors recommend individualized, periodic lactate testing when setting training zones for women masters athletes
expected_limitations: Only seven studies reported lactate, mostly cross-sectional and treadmill-based
Mostly runners rather than cyclists

evidence.quote: Although findings were mixed, peak lactate concentrations generally remained stable while lactate threshold as a percentage of VO2max increased with age.

These findings highlight the need for longitudinal research on lactate kinetics and em- phasize the importance of individualized, periodic lactate assessments when prescribing training zones in women masters athletes.
No significant differences in average lactate values during HIIT between younger and older subjects were detected.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-012 reviews lactate changes with age in women masters athletes. mcl-011 (lactate during sprint intervals similar in fitness-matched older and younger athletes of both sexes) and mcl-007 (lactate threshold declines less than VO2max with age) are related but not women-specific.

question: Do women and men masters athletes lose leg power at the same rate as they get older?
population_applicability: masters_athletes: elite track-and-field runners aged 35-90 at baseline (mcl-013, longitudinal) and master track cyclists aged 34-84 (mcl-002, cross-sectional)
expected_points: Over about 4.5 years of follow-up, declines in jump power, force and height were similar in men and women master athletes
In master track cyclists, sex had no significant effect on the age-related rate of decline in jump power or the other measures
Women athletes scored further above age- and sex-matched norms than men, while the advantage of power athletes was larger in men
expected_limitations: mcl-013 studied runners, not cyclists, with a mean follow-up of only 4.5 years
mcl-002 was cross-sectional and included only 15 women
Neither study followed a non-athlete control group

evidence.quote: We observed that over a mean of 4.5 ± 2.4 years changes in peak power, as well as force and jump height were similar in athletes of both disciplines and sexes.
Sex had no significant effect on the age-related rate of decline in any of the parameters (p = 0.985).
In addition greater EFI scores were observed in female power and endurance athletes than their male counterparts, even after adjustment for age and performance.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-013 follows leg power over time in both sexes and mcl-002 compares age-related decline by sex in master track cyclists; both answer directly. mcl-007 only notes that sex differences in endurance performance stay fairly stable with age, and mcl-001 does not measure leg power decline by sex.

question: Do older athletes who have done endurance training for years have stronger or more powerful legs than non-athletes their age?
population_applicability: masters_athletes: master distance runners (mcl-013 both sexes, baseline ages 35-90; mcl-014 men around 69) compared with age-matched norms or healthy older men; no cyclists
expected_points: Male master endurance runners had lower jump power than age- and sex-matched norms, while female endurance runners and power athletes scored above norms
Master runners around 70 had lower-leg muscle size and strength no different from healthy older men, and both groups were weaker than young men
Long-term endurance training alone did not reliably give stronger or more powerful legs; the clearest advantages were in power (sprint and jump) athletes
expected_limitations: Both studies are of runners, not cyclists
Cross-sectional comparisons with small groups (13 master athletes, men only, in mcl-014)
mcl-014 measured one shin muscle at low force; mcl-013 compared athletes with German reference data rather than a matched control group

evidence.quote: Male and female power athletes and female endurance athletes EFI scores were greater (all P < 0.01) and male endurance athlete scores lower (P = 0.01) than sex and age-matched normative values.

However, the data presented here demonstrate no substantial differences between healthy older individuals and master athletes, either in terms of muscle size and strength or motor unit numbers and structure, indicating that, contrary to expectation, master athletes are not protected from age-related motor unit remodeling.

No significant difference was apparent between OC and MA in bilateral knee extension 1RM strength and total exercise volume completed (the product of sets × repetition × load) was similar between OC and MA.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-013 gives leg power of master endurance runners against age norms and mcl-014 gives lower-leg muscle size and strength against healthy older men; together they cover power and strength, which neither covers alone. mcl-010 (similar knee-extension strength in a small group) and mcl-007 (review citing preserved muscle in master athletes) are partial; mcl-002 has no non-athlete comparison.

question: As people age and lose some of the nerve supply to their leg muscles, how do the muscles manage to keep their size?
population_applicability: older adults: healthy older men (mean 71) and male master runners (mean 69) compared with young men (mean 26)
expected_points: Surviving motor nerves take over muscle fibres that lost their nerve supply, so remaining motor units become larger (43% and 56% larger potentials in older men and master athletes than in young men)
This compensation kept shin muscle size similar to that of young men despite an estimated loss of motor units
Compensation is incomplete: older muscles produced less force for their size, possibly because of more non-contractile tissue, and master athletes were no different from non-athletes
expected_limitations: Small cross-sectional study of men only (18 young, 14 old, 13 master athletes)
Only the tibialis anterior was studied, at 25% of maximal force, so mainly smaller motor units were sampled
Motor unit numbers are estimates from EMG methods

evidence.quote: Intramuscular MUPs of Old and Master Athletes were 43% and 56% larger than Young.

The increase in iMUP and NF MUP size in the older participants shown here is an indication that reinnervation has compensated for the decrease in motor unit number and allowed muscle size to remain similar in Young and Old albeit, possibly, with more noncontractile material in the older muscles.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-014 is the only paper that measures motor unit size, motor unit numbers and muscle size together and explains the compensation. mcl-001, mcl-013 and mcl-007 discuss muscle or motor unit ageing but not how muscle size is preserved.

question: Do masters cyclists who swap heavy gym lifting for short all-out sprints on the bike keep their leg strength?
population_applicability: different population: young competitive cyclists (mean age about 29; 26 men and 2 women)
expected_points: After 6 weeks of short sprints instead of heavy lifting, half-squat 1RM fell by about 4% (3.9 ± 3.8%), while the group that kept lifting heavy gained about 9%
Short sprint training did not maintain strength gained from heavy lifting; the authors advise avoiding long periods without strength maintenance work
expected_limitations: Young trained cyclists, not masters
Only 6 weeks, no control group, and 28 cyclists in total

evidence.quote: From pre- to post test, the HST group increased load in the 1RM half-squat test by 9.1 ± 3.7%, from 125 ± 24 kg to 136 ± 25 kg (p < 0.001), while the SST group showed a 3.9 ± 3.8% decrease, from 128 ± 32 kg to 122 ± 30 kg (p = 0.001).

This mix of HST and SST training is indeed interesting, as our findings showed a 3.7% decrease in strength after 6 weeks of SST, indicating that SST does not satisfactorily maintain any HST-induced strength gain.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-015 directly tests what happens to strength when short sprints replace heavy lifting. mcl-017, mcl-004 and mcl-020 discuss keeping strength with about one session a week but do not test sprint work as a substitute.

question: Does adding heavy leg strength training make cyclists gain body weight or bulk up?
population_applicability: general trained cyclists: mostly young adult men (mcl-015 mean age about 29); no masters-specific data
expected_points: In trained cyclists, 6 weeks of heavy strength training increased maximal strength with no change in body mass, body fat or muscle mass
Studies reviewed in mcl-016 found larger thigh muscles without increased body mass, and performance improved even relative to body mass, in both women and men
expected_limitations: The 6-week intervention (after a 4-week preparation phase) may have been too short for muscle growth
Data come from younger cyclists, not masters; mcl-016 is a narrative review relying mainly on the authors' own studies

evidence.quote: No difference within groups was found in body mass (kg) (SST: p = 0.055, HST: p = 0.339), body fat (%) (SST: p = 0.856, HST: p = 0.157) or muscle mass (kg) (SMM) (SST; p = 0.302, HST; p = 0.215).
The specific effects of HST led solely to higher 1RM strength, without any indications of hypertrophic response.

In fact, in our studies we do not report increased body mass despite significant increases in quadriceps muscle CSA, and performance is also improved when adjusted for body mass in both female [2] and male cyclists [1].

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-015 measured body mass and muscle mass after heavy strength training and mcl-016 reviews studies showing muscle growth without body mass gain; both answer directly. mcl-020 reports cyclists' divided views on muscle gain; mcl-017 and mcl-004 report no body mass outcomes.

question: Does strength training help cyclists produce more power at the end of a long ride, when they are already tired?
population_applicability: different population: trained male and female cyclists (not masters-specific; ages not reported in the review)
expected_points: After 11-12 weeks of heavy strength training, both male and female cyclists raised average power in a 5-min all-out test done straight after a 3-hour submaximal ride by about 7%, with no such change in control cyclists
Oxygen use and heart rate were lower in the last part of the long ride, i.e. cycling economy improved late in the ride, which probably meant less fatigue before the final effort
The economy benefit may only show up in a fatigued state, not at the start of a ride
expected_limitations: Men and women were tested in separate studies by the same group, not compared directly in one study
Small samples of trained cyclists; the review does not address masters
Not every study finds better efficiency during long rides

evidence.quote: The improved cycling economy during the last part of this prolonged trial probably led to a lower magnitude of fatigue at the end of the trial, and both the male and female cyclists increased average power output in the following 5-min performance test to the same degree after the strength training program (men: 7.2 ± 6.6%, women: 7.0 ± 4.5%, Figure 1).
Both had reduced oxygen consumption and hence improved cycling economy during the last part of the submaximal trial, compared to before the strength training intervention and the control groups.

Therefore, it is possible that, at the beginning of a moder- ate intensity effort, in some cases, there may not be a clear difference in cycling efficiency after a heavy strength train- ing programme, but may be noticeable in a fatigued state.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-016 reports the 3 h ride plus 5-min test in both sexes. mcl-017 discusses the same fatigued-state findings but its meta-analysis covers only fresh-state efficiency, and mcl-015 has an end-of-test 5-min effort without a no-strength control group, so both get 1.

question: Will a short or light gym routine, such as a few weeks of squats only or explosive lifting, make a cyclist faster?
population_applicability: different population: trained male and female cyclists (not masters-specific; ages not reported in the review)
expected_points: Studies in which cyclists added heavy strength training (several leg exercises, about 4-12 repetition maximum, for at least 8 weeks) improved cycling performance
Programs that were short, low in volume or used explosive strength training failed to improve performance
One study of female cyclists that used only parallel squats found no benefit, probably because the training volume was too low
expected_limitations: Narrative review, not a systematic comparison of program doses
The meta-analysis found no significant moderating effect of program duration or weekly frequency, with low certainty of evidence

evidence.quote: In contrast, studies that included strength training programs of either short duration, included a low volume of strength training, or used explosive strength training [7,21–23] failed to show improved performance.
However, this might be because the strength training program only included one strength training exercise, making the total strength training volume too low for beneficial effects to occur [8].
Although we found no moderating effect of participants characteristics and strength training intervention on the variables analysed, it is important to mention some points.

annotation.author: Claude (AI draft)
annotation.rationale: mcl-016 directly contrasts heavy multi-exercise programs with short, low-volume or explosive ones. mcl-017 is related: its moderator analysis found no effect of duration or frequency.

question: If a cyclist stops lifting weights when racing starts, how long do the benefits last, and how much lifting is needed to keep them?
population_applicability: different population: adult endurance cyclists, mean age 31 (study means 19.5-51.5)
expected_points: Effective programs may need about 8 weeks with 2 sessions per week, and the effects may last up to about 6-8 weeks after strength training stops
In one included study, after a 12-week build phase of 2 sessions per week, 1 session per week during a 13-week competition period was enough to keep the gains
Without maintenance, the performance benefits seem to fade within about 8 weeks
expected_limitations: Based on few studies; low certainty of evidence
